items.prompt: White to move. Capture one of Black's pawns with the rook.

claims.statement: The rook can slide to a4 and take the pawn.
The rook can slide up the file to d7 and take the pawn.
Nothing defends the pawn on a4.
Nothing defends the pawn on d7.

hints: Which black pieces stand on a line the rook can travel along?
The rook moves along ranks and files. Look along the 4th rank and the d-file.
Either the pawn on a4 or the pawn on d7 can be taken.
items.explain: The rook captures the way it moves: it slides along a rank or file and lands on the enemy piece. Both pawns can be taken, a4 along the 4th rank and d7 up the d-file, and nothing defends either, so the rook is safe afterwards.

items.prompt: White to move. The knight can capture one black piece. Find the move.

claims.statement: The knight can jump to e6 and take the bishop.
No black piece defends the bishop.
Nxe6 wins the bishop and White keeps the knight.

hints: A knight jumps in an L shape. Which black piece is an L-jump away from the knight?
From d4 the knight reaches b3, b5, c2, c6, e2, e6, f3 and f5. One of those squares holds a black piece.
The bishop stands on e6.
items.explain: The knight on d4 jumps to e6, where the bishop stands, and takes it. No black piece can capture on e6, so the knight is safe there and White has won 3 points.

items.prompt: White to move. The pawn on d4 can capture something. Find the move.

claims.statement: The pawn can capture diagonally on e5.
The pawn cannot capture straight ahead; d5 is blocked.
Nothing defends the bishop on e5.
dxe5 wins the bishop for nothing.

hints: A pawn moves straight, but it captures in a different way. Which way?
A pawn captures one square diagonally forward. Look at c5 and e5.
The bishop on e5 can be taken by the pawn on d4.
items.explain: A pawn captures one step diagonally forward, never straight ahead, so the black pawn on d5 is simply in its way. The bishop on e5 is on a capturing diagonal and nothing defends it, so the pawn wins a bishop.

feedback_by_move.d4d5: The pawn cannot move onto d5: it is occupied, and pawns do not capture straight ahead.

items.prompt: Should White take the pawn on b5 with the rook? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: The pawn on a6 defends b5.
Rxb5 axb5 gives a rook for a pawn.

hints: Can the rook reach b5? Yes. Now ask what Black can do after.
Which black piece could take a rook standing on b5?
Look at the pawn on a6: which squares does it capture on?
items.explain: The rook can take on b5, but the pawn on a6 defends that square, so Black takes the rook back. White has given a rook (5 points) for a pawn (1 point), a loss of about 4 points.

items.prompt: Should White take the queen on b5 with the knight? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: The pawn on a6 defends the queen.
Nxb5 axb5 wins at least 5 points.

hints: Is the queen defended? Then count what each side gives up.
If Black takes back, which piece does Black take, and which piece did White take?
Count both sides: what does White give up, and what does White win?
items.explain: The pawn on a6 can take the knight back, so the queen is defended. But the knight is worth far less than the queen: White gives 3 points and wins 9, ahead by about 6. A defended piece can still be worth taking.

items.prompt: White to move. Should the knight take the pawn on e6? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: The rook on e8 defends the pawn on e6.
Nxe6 Rxe6 gives a knight for a pawn.

hints: Who could take back? Check files and diagonals all the way to the edge, not only the neighbours.
A rook can defend from far away if nothing stands in between. Look at the e-file.
The rook on e8 sees e6 through the empty square e7.
items.explain: The pawn on e6 has no neighbour, yet the rook on e8 defends it along the open e-file. After the knight takes, the rook takes the knight back: White gives 3 points for 1.

items.prompt: White to move. Should the bishop take the pawn on e5? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: The black king defends e5.
Bxe5 Kxe5 gives a bishop for a pawn.

hints: Who could take the bishop on e5?
Kings capture too. How close is the black king to e5?
Count every piece that touches e5, kings included.
items.explain: The king on e6 stands right beside e5, so after the bishop takes the pawn, the king takes the bishop: nothing else of White's guards e5, so the king may do it. White has given 3 points for 1.

items.prompt: White to move. Is Kxd4 a legal move? Predict, then check.

claims.statement: Kxd4 is not allowed.
The pawn on c5 defends d4.

hints: A king may never step onto a square an enemy piece attacks. Who attacks d4?
Black pawns capture diagonally downward. Which black pawn attacks d4?
Look at the pawn on c5: which squares does it attack?
items.explain: The black pawn on c5 attacks d4, so if the king took the pawn on d4 it would land on an attacked square. That is not allowed, so Kxd4 is illegal. A king can capture, but only a piece that nothing defends.

items.prompt: White to move. The bishop on c5 is loose. The pawn on d4 and the rook on c1 both seem to attack it. Which capture works? Find the move.

claims.statement: The pinned pawn cannot capture on c5.
The rook can take the bishop.
Nothing defends the bishop on c5.
Rxc5 wins the bishop for at most a pawn.

hints: Two white pieces seem to attack c5. Check that each one is free to move.
Look down the d-file: what stands behind the pawn on d4?
The rook on d8 pins the pawn to the king on d1, so only the rook may take.
items.explain: The pawn on d4 is pinned to the king by the rook on d8, so it may not capture. The rook takes the bishop. Taking with the cheapest piece only works when that piece is free to move.

feedback_by_move.d4c5: That move is illegal: the pawn on d4 is pinned against the king by the rook on d8.

items.prompt: White to move. The knight can take three black men. Only one capture wins material. Find it.

claims.statement: Nothing defends the bishop on c6.
Two black pieces defend the pawn on b5.
The pawn on f7 defends the pawn on e6.
Nxc6 wins the bishop.
Nxb5 loses material.

hints: Ask the capture question for each of the three black men: who could take back?
Two of the three are defended. Find the one that is not.
The bishop on c6 has no defender.
items.explain: Three captures are possible. The pawn on b5 is defended twice and the pawn on e6 once, so taking either loses the knight for a pawn. The bishop on c6 is loose, so the knight takes it for free.

feedback_by_move.d4b5: The pawn on b5 is defended by the pawn on a6 and the bishop on c6, so the knight would be lost for a pawn.
feedback_by_move.d4e6: The pawn on f7 takes back on e6, so the knight would be lost for a pawn.
